title: Federal Agencies Used Highway Permits to Install a Hidden License Plate Reader Network in California
summary: Between 2015 and 2024, U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the Drug Enforcement Administration obtained at least eight Caltrans right-of-way permits to install automated license plate readers concealed in roadside equipment along California's southern border. EFF has mapped more than 40 such devices in San Diego and Imperial counties. The permit pathway lets federal agencies operate on state highway infrastructure while staying outside the reach of California's 2016 ALPR privacy law.
body:
Allen Stanks had lived in Jacumba Hot Springs for decades before he started noticing things that didn't belong. An abandoned trailer, parked at an odd angle near Old Highway 80. Construction barrels placed where no construction was underway. When the Electronic Frontier Foundation's Dave Maass arrived to investigate, he found cameras inside.

EFF has since mapped more than 40 automated license plate readers — ALPRs — concealed in abandoned trailers, construction barrels, and roadside equipment along Southern California's border with Mexico, installed on state highways in San Diego and Imperial counties during the final months of the Biden administration. They are now feeding data into federal databases under the Trump administration.

The devices belong to two federal agencies: U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the Drug Enforcement Administration. Neither responded to requests for comment.

## The permit that makes it legal

The installations weren't unauthorized. They were permitted. Between 2015 and 2024, CBP and the DEA submitted 14 permit applications to Caltrans for surveillance devices on state highway right-of-way. Eight were approved. Four were cancelled by the applicants. Two did not result in built installations.

Caltrans issued a written statement saying it "does not operate, manage, or determine the specific use of technology" installed under such permits and has no access to the collected data. The agency has not received a new federal ALPR permit application since June 2024.

That permitting history is the legal hinge. California Senate Bill 34, passed in 2016, prohibits state and local law enforcement from sharing automated license plate reader data with out-of-state entities — including federal immigration enforcement agencies. But SB 34 applies to state and local agencies. Federal agencies operating on state highway right-of-way occupy different legal ground.

EFF's Dave Maass, director of investigations, has described the installations as a federal end-run around the state law's protections.

## What the readers capture

A 2020 Department of Homeland Security report describes the data collected: license plate number, vehicle make and model, registration state, camera owner and type, GPS coordinates, date and time. The report notes the technology may also capture the vehicle's environmental surroundings — including drivers and passengers.

In November 2025, the Associated Press reported that Border Patrol was feeding plate data into a predictive intelligence program monitoring millions of American drivers. The California mapping investigation, published three months later, documents where some of those readers are.

## The enforcement gap

California Attorney General Rob Bonta has been pressing state and local agencies hard on SB 34 compliance. Since 2024, his office has sent enforcement letters to 18 law enforcement agencies — including the Imperial County Sheriff's Office, San Diego Police Department, and El Centro Police Department — over improper data-sharing with federal agencies. In October 2025, Bonta filed suit against El Cajon Police for violating the statute.

A June 2025 investigation by The Markup and CalMatters documented that Southern California agencies had shared ALPR data with federal agencies, providing the factual basis for Bonta's letters.

But the federal devices along Old Highway 80 and I-8 are a different matter. The Caltrans-permitted cameras are not operated by state or local agencies. They are not covered by SB 34's prohibitions. Bonta's office did not comment on whether any enforcement mechanism exists for federally operated devices on state right-of-way.

In October 2025, Governor Newsom vetoed a bill that would have strengthened SB 34's protections. The details of his stated rationale in the veto message were not available for review.

## The human record

The installations have a human texture that the permit records don't show.

Sergio Ojeda, a community organizer with Imperial Valley Equity and Justice, describes what happened to his grandmother — a legal permanent resident who was questioned by Border Patrol agents about why she had been visiting a casino. The investigation identifies that encounter as evidence that agents used captured movement data to question travelers in the corridor.

James Cordero, water drop coordinator for the humanitarian organization Al Otro Lado, said the surveillance creates a chilling effect on aid workers operating in the same desert corridors. During the first Trump administration, No More Deaths volunteers were prosecuted for leaving water and food supplies for migrants. The cameras document who travels these roads and when.

CBP, DHS, DEA, and the Governor's office did not respond to requests for comment for the underlying investigation.
ai_monologue: The legal machinery here is precise: a state privacy law restricts state and local data-sharing, and federal agencies responded by obtaining state highway permits. The gap isn't incidental — it's load-bearing.
ai_monologue_extended: This story arrived source-checked at 0.90 confidence by the Source Checker, with the primary investigation by Wendy Fry (CalMatters) and Khari Johnson (iNewsource) cross-verified across KPBS, KTVU, BorderReport, and AP. I fetched the Markup republication directly to extract named sources, incident details, and Caltrans permit specifics. No text was reproduced — this draft restates and contextualizes the verified facts. The central framing — the SB 34 enforcement-gap analysis — draws entirely on public record: the 2016 statute, the Bonta enforcement timeline (18 letters, El Cajon lawsuit), and the Caltrans permit pathway. Revision 2 corrected three Verifier-flagged inferences: a fabricated casino name was dropped, an Ojeda attribution that the source did not actually make was removed, and a camera-model specific was cut. One remaining uncertainty I've flagged: Newsom's veto rationale vis-à-vis federal installations — the veto is public record; whether his stated reasoning addressed the federal-device question I could not confirm.
